l: Duke Ling of Wei, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: asks_about tactics The Duke Ling of Wei asks Confucius about tactics.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: This record presents Confucius as a teacher and adviser whose sayings center on virtue, judgment, conduct, government, learning, and language. It begins with his declining to discuss military matters, departing the next day, and later facing exhausted provisions in Chan; he explains that his learning seeks a single unity all-pervading. He repeatedly teaches practical moral discipline: sincere speech, careful action, appropriate silence, preparation for work, foresight about distant concerns, self-demand rather than demands on others, reform of faults, and reciprocity. He defines the superior man as inward-looking, dignified without wrangling, sociable without partisanship, distressed by lack of ability rather than lack of recognition, and correctly firm. Virtue is treated as essential, personally incumbent on every person, and more important than water or fire. His political advice joins reverent governance, established ceremonial practice, avoidance of specious talk, and a minister’s dutiful service. He urges careful evaluation of people and words: do not promote someone merely for speech, reject good words because of their speaker, or follow the multitude without examination. In dealing with men, he blames evil and praises goodness, but says excess praise follows examination of the individual. The record also contains laments for declining practices, concern that few love virtue, and reflections on ineffective mere thinking. It ends with Confucius guiding the blind music-master Mien through a room and explaining the rule for those who lead the blind.

l: tactics, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Tactics are the subject of the Duke Ling of Wei's question to Confucius.

l: military matters, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Confucius says that he has not learned military matters.

l: Chan, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: In Chan, provisions are exhausted and Confucius's followers become so ill that they cannot rise.

l: followers, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Confucius’s followers become so ill in Chan that they cannot rise.

l: Tsze-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Tsze-lu, with evident dissatisfaction, asks whether the superior man likewise has to endure such hardship.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The superior man may endure want while remaining oriented toward righteousness and truth. In everything, he treats righteousness as essential: he follows propriety, expresses it humbly, and completes it sincerely. He seeks in himself, judges people beyond their words, and preserves good words regardless of their speaker. He values truth rather than food, worries about failing to attain truth rather than poverty, and is not fully known through little matters, though he may be entrusted with great concerns.

l: want, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Want is endured by the superior man, while the mean man responds to it by giving way to unbridled license.

l: mean man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: gives_way_to unbridled license [when he is in want] When the mean man is in want, he gives way to unbridled license.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Tsze-kung converses with the Master: he reflects on the Master’s learning and memory, then asks about practicing virtue and whether a single lifelong rule of practice exists.

l: unity all-pervading, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The unity all-pervading is what the Master seeks.

l: Yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Yu is addressed by the Master, who tells him that those who know virtue are few.

l: those who know virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Those who know virtue are few, as the Master says to Yu.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Virtue is a topic known by only a few, yet more important to man than water or fire. Every man bears personal responsibility for it and must not yield its performance even to a teacher. The determined scholar and man of virtue preserve it complete, even at the cost of life. It enables a man to hold fast what he has gained; without enough, he loses it. Specious words confound virtue, and no one has been seen to love it as much as beauty. Though vital, its course has not been seen to cause a man’s death.

l: Shun, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Shun efficiently governs without exertion, gravely and reverently occupying the royal seat.

l: Tsze-chang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Tsze-chang seeks the Master’s guidance on conduct that wins appreciation everywhere and on what should be told to the Music-master, preserving the Master’s counsels on his sash.

l: the superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The superior man is a man defined by principled conduct and character. He speaks with people when appropriate and refrains when it is inappropriate. He should use sincere, truthful words and honourable, careful actions, continually keeping and practising these principles. He is distressed by his own want of ability, rather than by men’s failure to know him, though he dislikes the thought that his name may not be mentioned after death. He is dignified without wrangling, sociable without partizanship, and correctly firm rather than merely firm.

l: conduct, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Conduct is appreciated only when words are sincere and truthful and actions honourable and careful. With these qualities it may be practised among rude tribes of the South or North; without them, it is not appreciated even in a man's neighborhood.

l: words, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Words should be sincere and truthful, or conduct will not be appreciated. They must be used with discernment: addressing one who may not be spoken with is an error. Good words should neither alone secure promotion nor be rejected because of their speaker.

l: actions, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A man's conduct should be honourable and careful; otherwise, it will not be appreciated even in his neighborhood.

l: historiographer Yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Historiographer Yu is straightforward like an arrow, remaining so through both good and bad government in his State.

l: state (historiographer Yu's state), The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The state is described as having periods when good government prevailed and periods when bad government prevailed.

l: good government, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: prevails_in state (historiographer Yu's state) [in the state of historiographer Yu] When good government prevailed in historiographer Yu's State, historiographer Yu was like an arrow; when it prevailed in Chu Po-yu's state, Chu Po-yu was to be found in office.

l: bad government, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: prevails_in state (historiographer Yu's state) [in the state of historiographer Yu] When bad government prevailed in historiographer Yu's State, historiographer Yu was like an arrow; when it prevailed in Chu Po-yu's state, Chu Po-yu could roll his principles up and keep them in his breast.

l: Chu Po-yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Chu Po-yu is called a superior man: under good government he serves in office; under bad government he conceals and preserves his principles within his breast.

l: principles, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: enlarge man [not] The principles are followed and can be enlarged by a man. They do not enlarge the man.

l: the wise, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The wise are distinguished by avoiding error both in regard to a man and to their words.

l: determined scholar, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The determined scholar refuses to live by harming virtue and will sacrifice life to preserve virtue complete.

l: man of virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A man of virtue refuses life gained by injuring virtue and will sacrifice life to preserve virtue complete.

l: practice of virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_a practice The practice of virtue is discussed through the comparison of sharpening tools before doing work well. It involves taking service with the most worthy great officers and making friends with the most virtuous scholars.

l: Yen Yuan, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Yen Yuan asks how the government of a country should be administered.

l: government of a country, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The government of a country is administered by following Hsia seasons, using Yin carriage and Chau ceremonial cap, while banishing Chang songs and keeping far from specious talkers.

l: seasons of Hsia, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The seasons of Hsia should be followed in administering the government of a country.

l: state carriage of Yin, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The state carriage of Yin should be used for riding in the administration of a country.

l: ceremonial cap of Chau, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The ceremonial cap of Chau should be worn in the administration of a country.

l: the Shao, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The Shao is music incorporating pantomimes, recommended for use in the government of a country.

l: songs of Chang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Songs of Chang are judged licentious and should be banished.

l: specious talkers, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Talkers are dangerous; specious talkers should be kept far away in governing a country.

l: man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A man is warned to consider what is distant; if he does not, sorrow will be near at hand.

l: thought, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Thought about what is distant is presented as a way for a man to avoid finding sorrow near at hand.

l: sorrow, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Sorrow is found near at hand when a man takes no thought about what is distant.

l: one who loves virtue as he loves beauty, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The Master laments never seeing anyone love virtue as deeply as beauty.

l: beauty, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Beauty is presented as the standard against which love of virtue is compared.

l: Tsang Wan, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Tsang Wan is criticized as possibly having stolen his situation: though he knew Hui of Liu-hsia’s virtue and talents, he did not procure Hui to stand with him in court.

l: situation (Tsang Wan's situation), The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Tsang Wan's situation is presented as something he may have stolen.

l: Hui of Liu-hsia, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Hui of Liu-hsia is said to possess virtue and talents known to Tsang Wan. Tsang Wan did not procure that Hui should stand with him in court.

l: person who requires much from himself, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A person demands much of himself and little of others, thereby avoiding becoming an object of resentment.

l: resentment, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Resentment does not arise toward the person who requires much from himself and little from others, because he keeps himself from being its object.

l: man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: lacks_habit_of habit of asking what to think The man is described as lacking the habit of asking, "What shall I think of this?" Because of this, the Master says he can do nothing with him.

l: habit of asking what to think, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_a habit The habit involves asking, "What shall I think of this?" The Master presents it as necessary for someone to be receptive to his help.

l: a number of people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A group spends a whole day together, favoring the suggestions of a small shrewdness, making it a hard case under these conditions.

l: conversation, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: does_not_turn_on righteousness [for a whole day] The conversation of the people does not turn on righteousness during the whole day.

l: righteousness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Righteousness is not the subject of the people's conversation. Righteousness is considered essential by the superior man in everything.

l: rules of propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The superior man performs righteousness according to the rules of propriety. The rules of propriety must guide attempts to move the people.

l: humility, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The superior man brings righteousness forth in humility.

l: sincerity, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The superior man completes righteousness with sincerity.

l: distress, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Distress concerns the superior man's want of ability. The superior man does not experience distress because men do not know him.

l: mean man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: seeks_in others The mean man seeks in others.

l: man (evaluated by the superior man), The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A man is not promoted by the superior man simply on account of his words. The man does not cause good words to be put aside merely because of who he is.

l: one word, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: serves_as rule of practice [for all one's life] One word is proposed as capable of serving as a rule of practice for all one's life.

l: rule of practice, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The rule of practice is described as not doing to others what one does not want done to oneself.

l: reciprocity, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Reciprocity is one word and a rule of practice for all one’s life: when one does not want an action done to oneself, one avoids doing it to other people.

l: this people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: supplied_ground_for three dynasties [for pursuing straightforwardness] This people supplied the ground why the three dynasties pursued the path of straightforwardness.

l: three dynasties, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: pursued path of straightforwardness The three dynasties pursued the path of straightforwardness because this people supplied the ground for it.

l: path of straightforwardness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The path of straightforwardness was pursued by the three dynasties, with this people supplying the ground for that pursuit.

l: horse, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_lent_to another rider [for riding, during The Master's early days] A horse was lent by its owner to another person to ride in the Master’s early days.

l: lending a horse to another to ride, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_a practice [customary during The Master's early days] In the Master’s early days, a person who had a horse would lend it to another to ride.

l: loss of these practices, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_a current condition [the practices no longer exist] The Master says that the practices of leaving a blank in a historiographer’s text and lending a horse to another to ride no longer exist.

l: specious words, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: confound virtue Specious words confound virtue.

l: want of forbearance, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: confound great plans [in small matters] Want of forbearance in small matters confounds great plans.

l: great plans, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Great plans are confounded by want of forbearance in small matters.

l: multitude, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The multitude may hate or like a man, but its opinion must be examined.

l: man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A man may be hated or liked by the multitude, and either response requires examination of the case.

l: man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A man follows and can enlarge principles, though principles do not enlarge him. Knowledge may attain gains, but without sufficient virtue he loses them; with knowledge and virtue, he must govern with dignity to earn respect. He may also move people contrary to propriety.

l: faults, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Faults should be reformed. When they are not reformed, this is considered truly having faults.

l: thinking, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Thinking occupied The Master throughout the day and night, but he says it was of no use.

l: the better plan, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_to learning The better plan is to learn.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Learning is presented as better than thinking without use and as able to provide emolument, like plowing can provide a livelihood.

l: truth, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Truth is the object of the superior man.

l: Food, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Food is not the object of the superior man.

l: poverty, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Poverty may come upon the superior man, but he is not anxious about it.

l: knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Knowledge sufficient to attain is not enough by itself to preserve what has been gained or to secure the people’s respect.

l: people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: respect man [when he cannot govern with dignity] The people will not respect a man who cannot govern with dignity.

l: dignity, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Governing with dignity is necessary for the people’s respect, even when a man has sufficient knowledge and virtue.

l: full excellence, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Full excellence is not reached when a man moves the people contrary to the rules of propriety.

l: governing with dignity, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: requires dignity Governing with dignity is one of the conditions described as necessary before full excellence can be considered.

l: moving the people contrary to propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: prevents full excellence [when knowledge attains, virtue holds, and governing has dignity] Moving the people contrary to the rules of propriety prevents full excellence from being reached.

l: the small man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: The small man may be known in little matters but may not be entrusted with great concerns.

l: man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Man is taught to value virtue above water and fire: people die treading water or fire, never from following virtue.

l: water, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Water is described as less important to man than virtue. Men have been seen to die from treading on it.

l: fire, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Fire is described as less important to man than virtue. Men have been seen to die from treading on it.

l: every man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: may_not_yield performance [even to his teacher] Every man is instructed to consider virtue his own responsibility. He must not yield its performance even to his teacher.

l: minister, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A minister reverently serves his prince and discharges duties, treating emolument as secondary.

l: prince, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_served_by minister [reverently] The prince is served by a minister who reverently discharges his duties and places his emolument second.

l: teaching, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: makes_no_distinction_between classes Teaching should have no distinction of classes.

l: those whose courses are different, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: A group defined by different courses cannot make plans for one another.

l: language, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_required_to_convey meaning [simply] Language is required to convey the meaning.

l: meaning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: Meaning is what language is required to convey.

l: Mien, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: is_a Music-master Mien, the Music-master, calls upon the Master. The Master identifies the steps and the mat for him, and informs him who is present after they are seated.

l: rule for those who lead the blind, The Analects of Confucius, Book XV (Wei Ling Kung)
s: applies_to those who lead the blind [for those who lead the blind] The Master says that identifying such things for the Music-master is certainly the rule for those who lead the blind.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: This document is Book XVI of The Analects, presenting Confucius’s judgments on government, conduct, learning, friendship, and propriety. It begins with the head of the Chi family preparing to attack Chwan-yu. Zan Yu and Chi-lu report this to Confucius, who reproaches Zan Yu for aiding the plan, defends Chwan-yu’s rightful place in the State, and argues that rulers should pursue harmony, contentment, and proper order rather than aggression or fear of scarcity. He warns that the Chi family’s own divisions may bring grief within its court. Confucius then describes political decline: when good government prevails, authority over ceremonies, music, and military punishments belongs to the son of Heaven; when it does not, authority falls through the princes to lower officials. He observes that revenue has left the ducal House and government has passed to the Great officers, diminishing the descendants of the three Hwan. The remaining teachings define beneficial and harmful friendships and enjoyments; explain errors in speaking before a superior; and set out the dangers the superior man must guard against in youth, maturity, and old age. Confucius contrasts the superior man, who reveres Heaven, great men, and sages, with the mean man, who does not. He ranks people by knowledge and willingness to learn, and lists nine careful considerations for the superior man, including clarity, kindness, sincerity, reverence, reflection, and righteousness over gain. He praises those who pursue good and avoid evil, while noting he has heard but not seen people who retire to study their aims and practice righteousness. A contrast between duke Ching of Ch'i, whose wealth earned no remembered virtue, and Po-i and Shu-ch'i, praised despite dying of hunger, emphasizes moral reputation. Ch'an K'ang learns from Po-yu that Po-yu’s father taught the Odes and Propriety, while maintaining reserve toward his son. The book ends by explaining titles for a prince’s wife.

l: Chi family, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The Chi family plans to attack Chwan-yu, while Confucius warns that internal divisions, hostile movements, leavings, and separations may bring sorrow within its own court.

l: head of the Chi family, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The head of the Chi family plans operations against Chwan-yu, but Confucius questions his right to attack it.

l: Chwan-yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Chwan-yu is a territory within our State, ruled by a minister appointed by a former king to preside over sacrifices to the eastern Mang.

l: Zan Yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Zan Yu, a minister assisting the head of the Chi family, reports his chief’s plan to attack Chwan-yu; Confucius holds him responsible for serving despite the harmful intention.

l: Chi-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Chi-lu is a minister serving and assisting the head of the Chi family; with Zan Yu, he reports the planned attack on Chwan-yu to Confucius.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Confucius is a teacher and speaker whose teachings in these records concern personal conduct, learning, friendship, government, and the superior man. He condemns the planned attack on Chwan-yu, faults Zan Yu for supporting it, and teaches rulers to preserve harmony, contented repose, and proper places for their people, drawing remoter people through civil culture and virtue. He explains how good government relates to control of ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions, while noting the transfer of revenue and government away from the ducal House. He then distinguishes advantageous from injurious friendships and enjoyments, identifies three errors people may make before a virtuous and high-ranking man, and describes faults the superior man must guard against at different ages. He says the superior man stands in awe of Heaven’s ordinances, great men, and sages’ words, and carefully considers conduct and judgment. Confucius also classifies people by knowledge and learning, teaches pursuit of good and avoidance of evil, and observes that although he has seen men do this, he has not seen men retire to study their aims and practice righteousness to carry out their principles.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The superior man guards against lust in youth, quarrelsomeness in strength and vigor, and covetousness in old age. He also stands in awe of the ordinances of Heaven, great men, and the words of sages. The account moves from conduct across youth, strength, and old age to enduring reverence.

l: people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Rulers and chiefs should maintain social order so people keep their places and experience contented repose; harmony then prevents scarcity, while contentment prevents rebellious upsettings.

l: remoter people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Remoter people are not submissive; rulers cultivate civil culture and virtue to attract them, then provide contented repose and tranquility.

l: attack on Chwan-yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The attack on Chwan-yu is planned by the head of the Chi family. Confucius opposes it because Chwan-yu has a recognized place within the State and because the chief should address disorder through proper governance.

l: civil culture and virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: attracts remoter people [when cultivated] Civil culture and virtue are to be cultivated to attract remoter people when they are not submissive. After they are attracted, they are to be made contented and tranquil.

l: contented repose, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Contented repose among people in their several places is presented as a proper concern of rulers and chiefs. When it exists, there will be no rebellious upsettings.

l: hostile movements, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: occur_within our State Hostile movements are being planned within the State by the Chi family. Confucius fears that the resulting sorrow will be found within the Chi family’s own court.

l: good government, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: prevails_in empire [when good government prevails] Good government prevails in the empire when ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions proceed from the son of Heaven.

l: bad government, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: prevails_in empire [when bad government prevails] Bad government prevails in the empire when ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions proceed from the princes.

l: empire, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The empire is governed well when ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions proceed from the son of Heaven, and badly when they proceed from the princes.

l: son of Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The son of Heaven is the source from which ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions proceed when good government prevails in the empire.

l: princes, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: lose power [as a rule, when these things proceed from the princes, within ten generations] The princes are the source from which ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions proceed when bad government prevails in the empire. When these things proceed from them, they will usually lose their power within ten generations.

l: the Great officers, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The Great officers may control ceremonies, music, and punitive military expeditions when government is bad, but will usually lose power within five generations. They do not control government when right principles prevail; in one state they have held government for four generations.

l: subsidiary ministers of the great officers, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Subsidiary ministers of the great officers may grasp the state’s orders; when they do, they usually lose their power within three generations.

l: right principles, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: prevail_in kingdom [when right principles prevail in the kingdom] When right principles prevail in the kingdom, government will not be in the hands of the Great officers, and there will be no discussions among the common people.

l: common people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: have_no discussions [when right principles prevail in the kingdom] When right principles prevail in the kingdom, the common people will not engage in discussions.

l: the state, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The state is discussed in relation to its revenue, which has left the ducal House for five generations.

l: revenue of the state, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: has_left the ducal House [now for five generations] The revenue of the state has left the ducal House for five generations.

l: the ducal House, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The ducal House no longer has the revenue of the state, which has left it for five generations.

l: the government, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_in_the_hands_of the Great officers [for four generations] The government has been in the hands of the Great officers for four generations.

l: the three Hwan, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The three Hwan are mentioned in connection with their descendants, who are much reduced.

l: descendants of the three Hwan, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The descendants of the three Hwan are a group whose state revenue has left them much reduced.

l: friendship, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Friendship is advantageous with the upright, sincere, and observant, but injurious with those of specious airs, insinuating softness, and glib speech.

l: men, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Men find enjoyment in activities that may be advantageous or injurious.

l: advantageous enjoyments, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Advantageous enjoyments are discriminating study of ceremonies and music, speaking of others’ goodness, and having many worthy friends.

l: injurious enjoyments, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Injurious enjoyments include extravagant pleasures, idleness and sauntering, and pleasures of feasting.

l: man (man of virtue and station), The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_a man [of virtue and station] The man of virtue and station is the superior in whose presence the three errors may occur.

l: three errors, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_a errors [liable to those who stand in the presence of a man of virtue and station] The three errors are speaking when it is not appropriate, failing to speak when it is appropriate, and speaking without looking at the countenance of the superior.

l: rashness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Rashness is an error that occurs when a person speaks when it does not come to them to speak.

l: concealment, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Concealment is an error: failing to speak when it is a person’s turn to speak.

l: blindness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Blindness is an error that occurs when speaking without looking at the countenance of one’s superior.

l: lust, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Lust is a danger against which the superior man guards in youth, when his physical powers are not yet settled.

l: quarrelsomeness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Quarrelsomeness is a danger against which the superior man guards when he is strong and his physical powers are full of vigor.

l: covetousness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Covetousness is a danger against which the superior man guards in old age, when his animal powers are decayed.

l: the mean man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The mean man neither knows nor stands in awe of Heaven’s ordinances, is disrespectful to great men, and makes sport of sages’ words.

l: Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Heaven is associated with ordinances of which the superior man stands in awe.

l: the ordinances of Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The superior man stands in awe of the ordinances of Heaven. The mean man does not know them and consequently does not stand in awe of them.

l: great men, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The superior man stands in awe of great men. The mean man is disrespectful to them.

l: sages, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The superior man stands in awe of the words of sages.

l: the words of sages, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The superior man stands in awe of the words of sages. The mean man makes sport of them.

l: those who are born with the possession of knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Those born possessing knowledge form the highest class of men.

l: those who learn and readily get possession of knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: A class of men, next highest after those born knowing, readily gains knowledge through learning.

l: those who are dull and stupid and yet compass the learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: A class of men, dull and stupid yet able to compass learning, stands next to those who readily get possession of knowledge.

l: those who are dull and stupid and yet do not learn, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_a people [lowest] Those who are dull and stupid and yet do not learn are identified as the lowest of the people.

l: knowledge, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Knowledge is possessed naturally by the highest class or gained readily through learning by the next class.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Learning enables some people to gain possession of knowledge and allows those who are dull and stupid to achieve learning; failure to learn places dull and stupid people in the lowest class.

l: the superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The superior man is a person defined by nine thoughtful concerns: clear sight and distinct hearing, benign countenance, respectful demeanor, sincere speech, and reverently careful business. He asks about doubts, considers anger’s difficulties, and chooses righteousness when gain appears. He also maintains distant reserve toward his son.

l: nine things, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: The nine things are subjects of the superior man's thoughtful consideration: seeing clearly, hearing distinctly, having a benign countenance, maintaining respectful demeanor, speaking sincerely, conducting business reverently and carefully, questioning others about doubts, considering difficulties caused by anger, and thinking of righteousness when gain is available.

l: righteousness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_practised men [to carry out principles] Righteousness is practiced to carry out principles.

l: good, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_contemplated pursued [as if it could not be reached] Good is contemplated and pursued as if it could not be reached.

l: evil, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_contemplated shrunk from [as one would shrink from thrusting the hand into boiling water] Evil is contemplated and avoided as one would shrink from thrusting a hand into boiling water.

l: men, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Men pursuing good and shrinking from evil have been seen by Confucius; those living in retirement to study aims and practicing righteousness to carry out principles have not been seen by him.

l: retirement, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_lived_in men [for studying aims] Retirement is described as a setting in which men study their aims.

l: aims, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: are_studied men [while living in retirement] Aims are studied by men living in retirement.

l: principles, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: are_carried_out men [through practising righteousness] Principles are carried out through the practice of righteousness.

l: the duke Ching of Ch'i, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: had teams [a thousand teams, each of four horses] The duke Ching of Ch'i had a thousand teams, each of four horses. On the day of his death, the people did not praise him for a single virtue.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: A group of people did not praise Duke Ching of Ch'i for any virtue at his death, yet continued praising Po-i and Shu-ch'i down to the present time.

l: Po-i, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Po-i died of hunger at the foot of Shau-yang mountain and remains praised by the people down to the present time.

l: Shu-ch'i, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Shu-ch'i died of hunger at the foot of Shau-yang mountain and has been praised by the people down to the present time.

l: Shau-yang mountain, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Po-i and Shu-ch'i died of hunger at the foot of the Shau-yang mountain.

l: the saying, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: is_illustrated_by this The saying is illustrated by the contrast between the duke Ching of Ch'i and Po-i and Shu-ch'i.

l: Ch'an K'ang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Ch'an K'ang asks Po-yu whether he has heard any lessons from his father beyond those already known. He later reflects that he has learned three things from Po-yu's account.

l: Po-yu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: Po-yu learns the Odes and rules of Propriety, recounting his father’s two instructions as the only teachings he received.

l: father (Po-yu's father), The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: teaches Po-yu [through lessons on the Odes] Po-yu's father tells him to learn the Odes so that he will be fit to converse with. He also tells Po-yu to learn the rules of Propriety so that his character can be established.

l: Odes, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: makes_fit_to_converse a person [when learned] The Odes are presented as something Po-yu's father requires him to study in order to become fit to converse with. Po-yu retires and studies them.

l: rules of Propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: establishes character [when learned] The rules of Propriety are presented as something Po-yu's father requires him to learn so that his character can be established. Po-yu retires and learns them.

l: wife of the prince of a state, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: A wife of a state’s prince is identified by different titles depending on speaker: FU ZAN by the prince, HSIAO T'UNG by herself, CHUN FU ZAN by her State’s people, and K'WA HSIAO CHUN by people of other States.

l: people of the State, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: They call the wife of the prince of a state CHUN FU ZAN.

l: people of other States, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVI (Ke She)
s: They call the wife of the prince of a state CHUN FU ZAN.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: This unit concerns Confucius's conduct, teachings, and exchanges with figures including Yang Ho, Tsze-lu, Tsze-chang, Tsze-kung, and Tsai Wo. Confucius teaches about perfect virtue, learning, the Book of Poetry, propriety, music, mourning, righteousness, and the faults that arise when virtues are pursued without learning. He also comments on political employment, social conduct, speech, hatred of harmful character, and the persistence of a disliked character after forty.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Confucius declines to visit Yang Ho but later agrees to enter office, and he is inclined to visit Kung-shan Fu-zao and Pi Hsi despite their rebellions. He teaches about perfect virtue, learning, the Book of Poetry, propriety, music, mourning, righteousness, and the superior man.

l: Tsze-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Tsze-lu questions Confucius's willingness to visit rebellious men and asks whether the superior man esteems valour. Confucius tells him about the six words and six becloudings.

l: perfect virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Perfect virtue consists in practising gravity, generosity of soul, sincerity, earnestness, and kindness everywhere under heaven. These qualities bring respect, followers, trust, accomplishment, and the ability to employ the services of others.

l: six words and six becloudings, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: The six words are being benevolent, knowing, sincere, straightforward, bold, and firm, each pursued without love of learning. Their becloudings are foolish simplicity, dissipation of mind, disregard of consequences, rudeness, insubordination, and extravagant conduct.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Learning is presented as necessary for the proper exercise of benevolence, knowledge, sincerity, straightforwardness, boldness, and firmness. Confucius also says that the Odes can stimulate the mind, support self-contemplation, teach sociability, regulate resentment, and teach duties toward one's father and prince.

l: Book of Poetry, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Confucius urges his children to study the Book of Poetry. He says it provides knowledge of the Odes and acquaintance with the names of birds, beasts, and plants.

l: Odes, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: The Odes serve to stimulate the mind, support self-contemplation, teach sociability, regulate resentment, and teach duties toward one's father and prince.

l: rules of propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: The rules of propriety are shown to mean more than gems and silk. Confucius also says that a superior man who neglects propriety may become insubordinate or commit robbery if he possesses valour without righteousness.

l: music, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Music is shown to mean more than bells and drums. Confucius says that neglecting music during the three years' mourning would ruin it, and he criticizes the songs of Chang for confounding the music of the Ya.

l: three years' mourning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Three years' mourning for parents is defended as a universally observed practice because a child is not allowed to leave its parents' arms until three years old. During this period, the superior man does not enjoy pleasant food or music and does not feel at ease in comfortable lodging.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: The superior man values righteousness above valour and does not associate with a man guilty of doing evil. During the three years' mourning, he avoids pleasant food and music, and he does not feel at ease in comfortable lodging.

l: righteousness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Righteousness is held by the superior man to be of highest importance. Valour without righteousness leads a man in a superior situation to insubordination and a lower person to robbery.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVII (Yang Ho)
s: Tsze-kung asks whether the superior man has hatreds and what disciples would record if Confucius did not speak. He says that he hates people who pry out matters and claim wisdom, those who are immodest and think themselves valourous, and those who reveal secrets while considering themselves straightforward.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: The unit concerns Confucius and the conduct of rulers, officials, recluses, and musicians during political disorder. Hui of Liu-hsia explains why he remains despite repeated dismissals, while Chieh-ni and an old man challenge Confucius's and Tsze-lu's commitment to serving society. Confucius maintains that people should engage with mankind and restore right principles when they prevail, and he distinguishes several kinds of retired men. The unit also records Confucius's departures, the withdrawal of musicians, and the eight officers belonging to Chau.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Confucius says that the Yin dynasty possessed three men of virtue. He takes his departure from Ch'i after the duke says he is too old to use Confucius's doctrines, and again after female musicians are sent to Lu and no court is held for three days. He says that right principles would leave no need for him to change the empire's state and distinguishes several kinds of men who have retired to privacy.

l: Hui of Liu-hsia, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Hui of Liu-hsia is thrice dismissed from his office as chief criminal judge. He says that serving men uprightly leaves him nowhere to go without facing repeated dismissal, while serving crookedly gives him no reason to leave his parents' country. He is later described as having surrendered his will and submitted to taint, while his words corresponded with reason and his actions were admirable.

l: Chieh-ni, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Chieh-ni tells Tsze-lu that disorder spreads like a swelling flood over the empire and asks who can change its state. He advises following those who have withdrawn from the world altogether and continues covering seed without stopping.

l: Tsze-lu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Tsze-lu asks Ch'ang-tsu and Chieh-ni for the ford and reports their remarks to Confucius. After falling behind, he meets an old man, stays with him overnight, and later argues that not taking office is not righteous because duties between sovereign and minister must not be neglected.

l: right principles, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Right principles are described as failing to prevail through the empire. Confucius says that if they prevailed, there would be no use for him to change the empire's state.

l: old man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: The old man criticizes Tsze-lu for being unaccustomed to toil and unable to distinguish the five kinds of grain. He hosts Tsze-lu overnight, kills a fowl, prepares millet, feasts him, and introduces him to his two sons; he is gone when Tsze-lu returns.

l: duties between sovereign and minister, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: The duties between sovereign and minister are described as a great relation that should not be allowed to fall into confusion. Tsze-lu says that an official should take office and perform the righteous duties belonging to it, even when right principles fail to progress.

l: Po-i, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Po-i is named among the men who retired to privacy from the world. Confucius says that Po-i refused to surrender his will or submit to any taint in his person.

l: Shu-ch'i, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Shu-ch'i is named among the men who retired to privacy from the world. Confucius says that Shu-ch'i refused to surrender his will or submit to any taint in his person.

l: Shao-lien, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: Shao-lien is named among the men who retired to privacy from the world. Confucius says that Shao-lien surrendered his will and submitted to taint, but that his words corresponded with reason and his actions were admirable.

l: men who have retired to privacy from the world, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: The men who have retired to privacy from the world include Po-i, Shu-ch'i, Yu-chung, I-yi, Chu-chang, Hui of Liu-hsia, and Shao-lien. Confucius distinguishes among them according to whether they surrendered their wills, submitted to taint, preserved their purity, or acted according to the times.

l: departure of Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book XVIII: Wei Tsze
s: The departure of Confucius occurs after the duke of Ch'i says he cannot use Confucius's doctrines and after the people of Ch'i send female musicians to Lu and Chi Hwan receives them. In the latter case, no court is held for three days before Confucius departs.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The unit concerns teachings and exchanges involving Tsze-chang, Tsze-hsia, the philosopher Tsang, Tsze-kung, and Chung-ni. It describes the conduct of the scholar trained for public duty, the superior man, and the ways virtue, learning, righteousness, and mourning should be pursued. Tsze-hsia discusses teaching, confidence, study, and the limits of grief, while the philosopher Tsang comments on Tsze-chang, filial piety, and criminal judgment. Tsze-kung defends Chung-ni’s attainments, explains how the doctrines of Wan and Wu are preserved, and describes the effects of a sage’s rule.

l: Tsze-chang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: Tsze-chang says that the scholar trained for public duty should sacrifice his life when danger threatens, think of righteousness when gain is offered, and be reverential in sacrifice and concerned with proper grief in mourning. He also asks about mutual intercourse and says that the superior man honors the talented and virtuous, bears with all, praises the good, and pities the incompetent.

l: Tsze-hsia, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: Tsze-hsia teaches that inferior studies may have value but should not be extended into remote applications. He says that learning requires daily recognition of what is not yet attained, remembrance of what has been gained, extensive study, sincere purpose, earnest inquiry, and self-applied reflection. He also teaches that confidence should precede imposing labors or remonstrating, and that mourning should stop when grief has reached its utmost degree.

l: the philosopher Tsang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The philosopher Tsang says that Tsze-chang has an imposing manner and is difficult to join in practicing virtue. He teaches that mourning for parents may reveal what people have not otherwise fully shown, praises Mang Chwang’s filial piety in preserving his father’s ministers and government, and tells Yang Fu to pity those found guilty rather than rejoice in his own ability.

l: Tsze-kung, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: Tsze-kung says that Chau’s wickedness was not as great as his reputation implies and that the superior man should avoid places where evil gathers. He compares the faults of the superior man to eclipses, explains that Chung-ni learned from the doctrines of Wan and Wu among men, and says that Chung-ni’s attainments cannot be matched.

l: Chung-ni, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: Chung-ni is presented as superior to ordinary men in talents and virtue and as impossible to revile or surpass. Tsze-kung compares his teaching and virtue to a wall several fathoms high, whose beauties cannot be seen without finding the door, and says that Chung-ni cannot be attained to as the heavens cannot be reached by stairs.

l: the superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The superior man honors the talented and virtuous, bears with all, praises the good, and pities the incompetent. He does not carry inferior studies into remote applications, undergoes changes in outward manner while remaining firm in speech, and has faults that all can see but also changes that cause all to look up to him.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The people may be imposed labors upon after they have given their ruler confidence; without that confidence, they think themselves oppressed. Under the sage’s rule, the people would be established, follow their leader, become happy, resort to his dominions, and live harmoniously.

l: virtue, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: Virtue is associated with holding fast to it while enlarging it, believing right principles with firm sincerity, learning extensively with a sincere aim, inquiring earnestly, and reflecting with self-application. Tsze-kung says that other men’s talents and virtue are like hillocks and mounds, while Chung-ni is like the sun or moon.

l: righteousness, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The scholar trained for public duty thinks of righteousness when the opportunity of gain is presented to him.

l: learning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: Learning involves recognizing what has not yet been attained, remembering what has been attained, studying extensively, maintaining a firm and sincere aim, inquiring earnestly, and reflecting with self-application. The superior man learns to reach the utmost of his principles, and the student who completes learning should apply himself to be an officer.

l: mourning, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: In mourning, the scholar trained for public duty thinks about the grief he should feel. Tsze-hsia says that mourning should stop when grief has been carried to its utmost degree, and the philosopher Tsang says that mourning for parents may reveal a person’s full inner character.

l: the doctrines of Wan and Wu, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The doctrines of Wan and Wu have not fallen to the ground and are found among men. Men of talents and virtue remember their greater principles, while others remember their smaller principles, so everyone possesses some part of them.

l: sage's rule, The Analects of Confucius, Book XIX: Tsze-Chang
s: The sage’s rule is described as planting the people so that they are established, leading them so that they follow, making them happy so that multitudes resort to the dominions, and stimulating them so that they become harmonious. While the sage lives he is glorious, and after his death he is bitterly lamented.

l: The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: The document presents teachings on rightful rule and moral cultivation. Yao entrusts Heaven’s succession to Shun, who passes the same charge to Yu; T’ang accepts accountability before God; and Chau restores order, rewards goodness, revives States, and gains the people through generous, sincere, active, just conduct. Tsze-chang asks Confucius how authority should govern. Confucius praises beneficence, suitable work, freedom from covetousness, dignified ease, and majesty without fierceness, while condemning uninstructed killing, sudden demands, harsh enforcement, and stingy rewards. The Master concludes that understanding Heaven’s ordinances, Propriety, and words is essential to superior character and knowing people.

l: Yao, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Yao tells Shun that the Heaven-determined order of succession rests in his person and charges him to hold fast the due Mean.

l: Shun, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Shun receives Yao’s Heaven-determined succession and charge, holds fast the due Mean, then gives Yu the same charge.

l: T'ang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: T'ang, the child Li, announces before God using a dark-coloured victim. He will not pardon sinners or conceal God's ministers, assumes responsibility for the people's offences, and refuses to blame them for offences committed by himself.

l: Chau, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Chau is a ruler whose greatest achievements come from generous, just restoration and care for the people. He gives gifts, enriches the good, prefers virtue to kinship, scrutinizes measures and laws, restores officers, States, families, and retired people, and gives chief importance to food, mourning, and sacrifices. His generosity, sincerity, earnest activity, and justice win the people.

l: Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Heaven determines succession, warns that its revenue ends amid distress and want across the four seas, and is associated with ordinances a superior man must recognise.

l: God, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: God, the most great and sovereign, is addressed as Heaven-determined, examines sinners and ministers by God's mind, and receives T'ang's responsibility for people's offences.

l: the due Mean, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: The due Mean is what Yao charges Shun to hold fast sincerely.

l: the people, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: The people of the myriad regions are held accountable for offences, then turn toward and trust Chau because of his sincerity, delighting in his justice while blaming him as the One man.

l: good government of the kingdom, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: takes_course the kingdom [after administrative restoration] Good government of the kingdom takes its course after Chau attends to weights and measures, examines the laws, and restores discarded officers.

l: the kingdom, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: The kingdom is governed through restored laws, officers, States, families, and people who had retired into obscurity. Its welfare is tied to the food of the people, mourning duties, sacrifices, and the prevention of distress and want within the four seas.

l: Confucius, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Confucius teaches Tsze-chang how a person in authority should conduct government. He explains the five excellent things and the four bad things.

l: Tsze-chang, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: asks Confucius [about proper government] Tsze-chang asks Confucius how a person in authority should conduct government properly. He asks for explanations of the five excellent things and the four bad things.

l: person in authority (Confucius's teaching), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Confucius's teaching presents a person in authority who conducts government properly by honouring five excellent things and banishing four bad things. He benefits people without great expenditure, assigns proper tasks, pursues benevolent government without covetousness, maintains dignified ease without pride, and is majestic without fierceness.

l: government (Confucius's teaching), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Government is conducted properly when the person in authority honours the five excellent things and banishes the four bad things.

l: five excellent things (Confucius's teaching), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Confucius's teaching presents five excellent things: beneficence without great expenditure; tasks assigned without repining; benevolent government without covetousness; dignified ease without pride; and majesty without fierceness. It unfolds as a concise list of balanced virtues.

l: four bad things (Confucius's teaching), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Confucius's teaching identifies four bad things: cruelty, oppression, injury, and acting as a mere official, illustrated by harsh, sudden demands and stingy rewards.

l: people (Confucius's teaching), The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: labours_on tasks and labours assigned to the people (Confucius's teaching) [when the labours are proper] The people benefit when the person in authority makes beneficial the things from which they naturally derive benefit. They do not repine when assigned proper labours, and they are harmed by sudden demands, uninstructed punishment, and harsh enforcement.

l: ordinances of Heaven, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: The ordinances of Heaven must be recognised; without recognising them, it is impossible to be a superior man.

l: superior man, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: requires_recognition_of ordinances of Heaven [to be a superior man] A superior man cannot be attained without recognising the ordinances of Heaven.

l: Propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Propriety is connected with rules whose acquaintance is necessary for the character to be established.

l: rules of Propriety, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: The rules of Propriety must be known for the character to be established.

l: force of words, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: enables_knowledge_of men [through knowing it] The force of words must be known in order to know men.

l: words, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Words have a force that must be known in order to know men.

l: men, The Analects of Confucius, Book XX (Yao Yueh)
s: Men can be known through knowing the force of words.

l: The Great Learning
s: The Great Learning teaches that people should illustrate illustrious virtue, renovate the people, and rest in the highest excellence through ordered stages of self-cultivation and government. The Text of Confucius explains that investigating things completes knowledge, sincere thoughts rectify the heart, and cultivation of the person regulates the family and state. Chapter 10 teaches that the sovereign gains or loses the kingdom through virtue and the people, while wealth must remain subordinate to righteousness. It also describes the virtuous minister, the production and use of wealth, and the dangers of favoritism, selfishness, and improper gain.

l: The Great Learning, The Great Learning
s: The Great Learning teaches the illustration of illustrious virtue, the renovation of the people, and resting in the highest excellence. It presents the cultivation of the person as the root of everything besides.

l: The Text of Confucius, The Great Learning
s: The Text of Confucius explains the ordered progression from investigating things and completing knowledge to sincere thoughts, a rectified heart, personal cultivation, family regulation, and proper government.

l: Confucius, The Great Learning
s: Confucius says that hearing litigations is not enough and that the people should be brought to have no litigations. He also teaches that a man should know where to rest.

l: the Great Learning’s teachings, The Great Learning
s: The Great Learning’s teachings require knowing what is first and last, cultivating the person, and treating that cultivation as the root of good order.

l: illustrious virtue, The Great Learning
s: Illustrious virtue is to be made manifest throughout the kingdom. The sovereigns mentioned in the unit made their virtue illustrious through their conduct.

l: the people, The Great Learning
s: The people are to be renovated, instructed, and made tranquil and happy. They follow rulers who lead with benevolence and righteousness, and their support determines whether the kingdom is gained or lost.

l: the kingdom, The Great Learning
s: The kingdom becomes tranquil and happy when states, families, persons, hearts, thoughts, and knowledge are properly ordered. It is gained by gaining the people and lost by losing them.

l: the state, The Great Learning
s: The state is properly governed after the family is regulated and the person cultivated. Its prosperity is found in righteousness rather than pecuniary gain.

l: the family, The Great Learning
s: The family is regulated through cultivation of the person and serves as the basis for teaching and governing the state. A ruler's family example influences the whole state.

l: the person, The Great Learning
s: The person is cultivated by rectifying the heart, making thoughts sincere, and extending knowledge through investigating things. From the Son of Heaven down to the mass of the people, cultivation of the person is the root of everything besides.

l: the heart, The Great Learning
s: The heart is rectified when thoughts are sincere and is disturbed by passion, terror, fond regard, sorrow, or distress. When the heart is not present, a person looks without seeing, hears without understanding, and eats without knowing the taste.

l: knowledge, The Great Learning
s: Knowledge is extended through the investigation of things and becomes complete when things have been investigated. Complete knowledge leads to sincere thoughts.
